newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Latin lover Mastroianni muses on old age, death.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Latin lover Mastroianni muses on old age, death.

text.p: Dressed in a shabby brown cardigan and slippers, Marcello Mastroianni shuffles to the middle of a bare and gloomy room and waters a pot of basil.
"Basil is not particularly beautiful," he says. "It's just very green and has a strong scent. I like the way it smells -- it smells of youth."
The 1960s screen star who turned a generation of women on to the thrill of the Latin lover has not fallen on hard times or lost himself in a fit of nostalgia.
He is on stage, poignantly playing a widower who moves to an old people's home and is too embarrassed, and too afraid of imposing, to admit he wants to go back and live with his son.
Mastroianni, now 72, was in Paris, discussing playing "another ageing Casanova", when he read the script of Italian dramatist Furio Bordon's play, "Le Ultime Lune" (The Last Moons).
"Maybe because I'm in the antechamber of some situations, I got so emotional reading it that I decided: Let's do it right away," he told an interviewer in Venice, where the play opened.

Illness put him out of action for a time but the Italian, who shot to fame in Federico Fellini's 1960 classic "La Dolce Vita", was back on stage with the play in Milan last month, drawing full houses and standing ovations.

A wave of Mastroianni nostalgia has followed, with the publication of a book based on his memories of a 50-year career spanning some 160 movies and a television special, "The Appeal of Normality", in which his co-stars poured out their affection.

"Every woman always had the idea it would have been easy to seduce him," said Italian actress Gina Lollobrigida, recounting how, on the set of "La Loi" (Where the Hot Wind Blows) in 1959, Marcello would mysteriously disappear in the evenings but return punctually the next morning with a smile.
In the interviews which make up Enzo Biagi's new book "La Bella Vita" (The Beautiful Life), however, Mastroianni portrays himself as a shy boy who just got lucky in life and love.

He didn't even look like a sex symbol -- "When I was a kid ...I had a chest that looked like a basket and two bird's legs," he said in 1967. "I'm not handsome and I never have been. I've got an ordinary face, anonymous, even a country bumpkin's face."
The New York Times Magazine once summed up his languid attitude, calling him "the man who made apathy irresistible".

Mastroianni, who was discovered as he acted in a university theatre company after the war and joined director Luchino Visconti's troupe, shouldn't have got the part in "La Dolce Vita" -- Paul Newman's was the preferred name in the frame.
He has never regarded himself as special. In 1971 he declared: "I smoke 60 cigarettes a day, I drink like a sponge...and my interests have never been all that important."
But the loyalty he has inspired in others is legendary.

Sophia Loren, his co-star in 12 films where the pair's chemistry and glamour created the iconic Italian couple, said theirs was a lasting partnership that meant "we don't have to rehearse any more". A cameo role in Robert Altman's 1994 movie "Pret a Porter", playing reunited ex-lovers, proved the point.
Their on-screen allure in films such as "Marriage Italian Style" and "Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" kept people guessing about real romance, but Mastroianni said nothing happened.
Thrust into the public eye beside Loren, film clips show an awkward Mastroianni shunning the flash of the paparazzi, a word coined by "La Dolce Vita", the film to which he owed his career.
The movie also kicked off a deep friendship with Fellini until the director's death in 1993. Fellini was his confidant and mentor. "Marcello is me," Biagi quoted Fellini as saying.
He routinely turns down press interviews today, perhaps afraid the world only wants lurid details about his love life.
"I'll never speak of the most intimate, most secret things," he told Biagi.

Mastroianni is frank about the facts, however. He married his wife, Flora, after a whirlwind romance and had a daughter, but ruled out divorce despite a string of affairs, including one with French movie goddess Catherine Deneuve, with whom he has another daughter, and a liaison with American Faye Dunaway.
He confessed to never having liked the "Latin lover" epithet but admitted life in the fast lane was fun.
"I've had luck, love, success, money. I've always spent it and I'll continue to do so," he said in 1994.

He has aged well. He is slim and smiling, though he stoops a little, and his familiar features are wrinkled. His mellow, gravelly voice on stage is as strong as ever but without his trademark heavy-rimmed spectacles, he can look tired and old.
Though in the popular imagination he is still "Il Bel Marcello", sometimes he sounds like the old man he now is.
His daughter Chiara holds his hand now when they cross the road in Paris, he said earlier this year.
As he has got older, Mastroianni admits that the thought of death increasingly distresses him. Illness during "Le Ultime Lune" just made him want to prove himself more.

"Turning 70 was a bad year for me," he said. "In Paris, I fell down the steps of the Italian consulate and broke six ribs, perforated my pleura, then there was a disc hernia, diabetes, labyrinthitis (ear infection), everything," he said.
"But then listen, I see a long film which started many years ago and is not finished yet," he told Biagi.
One press article saying he felt "the breath of death" cut him to the quick. His brother Ruggiero, who died this year, quipped he should buy a polo-necked sweater to keep it at bay.
Mastroianni says he hopes never to give up work, but what has shaped his life more than cinema were experiences of poverty after the war, of childhood friends, his youth and his family.
As one of the lines in Bordon's play echoes: "When you're old, you can even forget sex, but not sentiments."
